title: TEF with teeth? Why the OfS’s quality proposals need a ‘start again’ box
summary:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Sir Peter Scott, Emeritus Professor of Higher Education Studies at UCL, former Vice-Chancellor of Kingston University between 1998 and 2010 and the first Commissioner for Fair Access in Scotland.  The one box that never appears in consultations, despite often being the most important, is the one that says […]

The post TEF with teeth? Why the OfS’s quality proposals need a ‘start again’ box appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Sir Peter Scott, Emeritus Professor of Higher Education Studies at UCL, former Vice-Chancellor of Kingston University between 1998 and 2010 and the first Commissioner for Fair Access in Scotland.

The one box that never appears in consultations, despite often being the most important, is the one that says ‘I wouldn’t start from here’. Often, simply by responding to consultations, you can end up implicitly endorsing the fundamental shape of a future that has been pre-determined. Most consultations are designed to endorse, possibly tweak, not to contradict policies that have already been agreed. This is certainly true of the Office for Students’ second round consultation on quality.

In (very) brief the OfS is proposing initially to assess the quality of every single registered institution from Oxbridge to the latest ‘alternative provider’ in its rented office block; then subsequently assess institutions with ‘Gold’ awards in the Teaching Excellence Framework (TEF) every five years, those with a ‘Silver’ award every four years, those with a ‘Bronze’ award (or a ‘satisfactory’ outcome if they opt out of the TEF) every three years and all the rest ever two years; to restrict student numbers for institutions that do not get ‘Gold’ or ‘Silver’ awards; and, it seems, to cancel the registration of any institution that gets an ‘unsatisfactory’ grade two times running – two strikes and you are out.

As a result, the purpose of the TEF will be transformed, admittedly its purpose has never been entirely clear. It was established as a counterweight to the Research Excellence Framework (REF) to ensure that the interests of teaching were not swamped by those of research; hence the parallel name. But the parallel was symbolic rather than substantive. From the start it was clear that the TEF could not work in the same way, because it had no role in allocating funding. Until now: under the OfS’ proposal TEF results will be used to restrict institutional funding for institutions that do not receive ‘Gold’ or ‘Silver’ awards. ‘TEF with teeth’, as some commentators have described it.

The OfS’s proposed new quality regime suffers from a number of flaws, which cannot be addressed by tweaks. Instead, they can probably only be addressed by ticking the ‘I would not start from here’ box, which of course does not exist. First, the OfS is proposing to take on an administrative burden which the, now excluded (and, of course, independent), Quality Assurance Agency never attempted. Nor did the Office for Standards in Education (Ofsted) in the schools sector, even in its most aggressive phase. Many schools went longer than five years between inspections, the maximum to be allowed by the new OfS quality regime even for major research intensive universities. Just think of the mountains of data and, where required, the number of visits and battalions of assessors that will be required. Is any of this feasible?

Second, is the OfS’s proposed quality regime proportionate? The consultation paper has a lot to say about risk assessment, but the difference in treatment of institutions it proposes is modest. In practice, the great majority of well established public institutions pose few significant quality issues they cannot handle through their own traditional means. To subject them to constant assessments, perhaps undertaken by academic assessors whose credibility may not match that of those they are assessing and inevitably generating a compliance bureaucracy gobbling up resources badly needed for teaching and research, is simply a waste of money – and of everyone’s time. It is the ‘alternative providers’, often for-profit institutions subject to frequent changes of control and ownership which often have extremely limited academic track records, that are the main problem – and the few public institutions unwise (and hard up?) enough to have agreed to sub-contract with these providers through validation or franchising arrangements.

The previous Government, which had encouraged the growth of these providers on the hopeful grounds they would pioneer ‘innovation’ and equally hopeful grounds that they could widen participation in ways established institutions could not, would instinctively have resisted this conclusion. But the present Government’s hands are not tied in the same way. Attention, and resources, should be focused where the risks are likely to arise – unless the OfS is indulging on some undeclared fantasy to ‘drive up standards’ everywhere.

Third, the OfS seems to confuse compliance with quality, although it is really talking about standards. The quality of teaching, and student learning, cannot be assessed in terms of outputs such as continuation, completion and employment rates (perhaps with a dash of inputs, like staffing and resources). It cannot even be assessed through measures of student satisfaction, important as they are. Instead notions of quality are grounded within bodies of knowledge curated by expert practitioners. For example, is the teaching informed by relevant and up-to-date research in the case of academic disciplines – or the best professional practice in the case of vocational ones? Also, ‘TEF with teeth’ is clearly incompatible with using the framework for quality enhancement. The stakes will simply be too high. Quality enhancement needs to be focused on improvement, not compliance, and depends on respectful partnership, not bureaucratic enforcement.

Fourth, the OfS proposals make no attempt to address systemic risks, such as the threat AI presents to current patterns of assessment. Nothing on transnational education (TNE) or even postgraduate courses, both areas of greater systemic risk than mainstream undergraduate provision. It is hard to resist the suspicion that the OfS is stuck in a familiar groove, suspicious that universities will be guilty of sloppy teaching and/or disregard for their student customers unless kept up to the mark by permanent surveillance.

Finally, has the OfS considered the lawfulness of any decision to restrict student recruitment or cancel institutional registrations based on this process? Where in the Education and Research Act is the warrant for its expanded inspectorial role? The OfS does not have a good track record of defending judicial reviews, which would surely come from institutions that suffer detriment as a result of what they will argue is a flawed process. In the Sussex ‘free speech’ case, it was guilty of spectacular overreach.

Put simply the, OfS is proposing to out-Ofsted Ofsted, just when the latter agency has concluded that a more modest and consensual approach to schools inspection is more effective. By relying on TEF awards, it is proposing to use what are, in effect, single-word judgments, which are now widely accepted to be inadequate in the case of large secondary schools. How much more inadequate for higher education institutions with hundreds of academic programmes and (tens of) thousands of students. By managing the process itself, the OfS is running the risk of allowing quality judgments to be contaminated by policy goals, which it is also – rightly – pursuing (assuming it can avoid the outright politicisation of the Sussex case).

The OfS already faces a major task establishing trust among institutions, and staff and students. Post-Sussex it has, formally at any rate, acknowledged the importance of this task. These proposals on quality will make that more difficult. In the eyes of many, they amount to overreach – again. Surely the OfS will not be guilty, like the Bourbons in Talleyrand’s phrase, of learning nothing but remembering everything?

title: These maps show how expensive state schools can be for low-income students
summary:
To avoid spending their young adult lives in debt, students have long been counseled to stay in-state for college. After all, it’s the mission of public universities, funded by tax dollars, to provide an affordable, high-quality education to state residents.  Yet, in 34 states, it costs students from low-income families at least a third of […]

The post These maps show how expensive state schools can be for low-income students appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
To avoid spending their young adult lives in debt, students have long been counseled to stay in-state for college. After all, it’s the mission of public universities, funded by tax dollars, to provide an affordable, high-quality education to state residents.

Yet, in 34 states, it costs students from low-income families at least a third of their household income — upwards of $10,000 a year — to attend the state flagship university. That includes not just tuition, but also room and board and books, after accounting for all grants and scholarships — what’s known as “net price.”

Take Alabama, which had one of the highest price tags for public colleges in the country in 2024, the most recent data available. A student coming from a family in that state that earns less than $30,000 a year was expected to pay more than $19,000 annually on average for tuition and other costs at the University of Alabama, the flagship. The same went for Pennsylvania State University.

And it’s not just flagship universities. At more than half of four-year public colleges across the country, including regional public institutions as well as large research universities, in-state students from families making less than $30,000 faced this same, near-impossible financial juggling act: On average, they had to pay more than a third of their family income to attend.

Net price at public colleges has declined over the past few years, when adjusted to overall inflation, yet wages have not kept up as the costs of housing, food and health care keep rising, and low-income families continue to struggle to afford college.

Some states have done a better job of controlling costs than others. Florida — just across the state line from Alabama — had among the least expensive four-year public colleges in the country. That’s largely because the state legislature has maintained funding for higher education and capped tuition over the past decade.

Hover over the map to see the cost for each state.

Even if students from families earning less than $30,000 take out the maximum federal student loan allowed ($5,500 for first-year students), attending one of nearly 300 public four-year colleges still cost them at least $4,500 more in their first year alone, even when they stayed in-state. The same was true at more than 50 public two-year colleges that also offer bachelor’s degrees.

Hover over each dot to see the name of the college and the average cost.

The situation wasn’t much better for students from families making between $30,000 and $48,000. They needed to come up with a sizable share of their annual income, $5,000 — after all scholarships and maximum student loans — at close to 300 four-year public colleges, even when they enrolled in-state.

About 1 in 6 American households earns less than $30,000 a year. More than 1 in 4 earn less than $50,000.

State flagship universities boast some of the highest graduation and job placement rates among public universities, which makes them a crucial path to a secure financial future for students who grew up in poverty. Their affordability, however, depends on where you live.

Students from families who make less than $30,000 paid just over $1,000 out of pocket for tuition and other costs at the University of Michigan and roughly $2,000 at the state flagships in Florida, North Carolina and Illinois. Pennsylvania State University and the University of Alabama were the most expensive for low-income families, but the state flagships in New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oregon and Iowa all also cost students whose families make less than $30,000 more than half their annual income.

It’s not just the flagship that’s pricey in Alabama. The state’s other public colleges were among the most expensive in the country on average for families who make less than $48,000. (A spokesman from the University of Alabama said that the average net price for families making less than $30,000 dropped by about 6 percent in 2024-25, which brought it to about $18,000; it decreased by 12 percent for families making between $30,001 and $48,000, he said.)

The University of North Alabama, which cost low-income students the least in the state, still had a net price of close to $10,000. And half of Alabama’s public colleges cost more than $14,000 for students whose families make less than $30,000.

There are less expensive public colleges scattered around the country, and some students save money by starting at a community college and then transferring, although that path isn’t always available. At just over 60 public four-year colleges, the net price for families who make less than $30,000 was $5,000 or less in 2024. New York City, where most students don’t live on campus, hosts seven colleges that cost less than $1,600.

Contact senior investigative reporter Meredith Kolodner at kolodner@hechingerreport.org or on Signal: @merkolodner.04.

This story about college cost was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education. Sign up for our higher education newsletter.

title: 5 Findings on Gen Z’s Changing Priorities
summary:
5 Findings on Gen Z’s Changing Priorities
Joshua.Bay Tue, 11/24/2026 - 03:00 AM

New research reveals the challenges and opportunities facing young people, from improving mental health to navigating growing AI use and economic pressures.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
The evolving priorities, challenges and expectations of Gen Z are shaping how they navigate college and prepare to enter the workforce.

Recent research shows signs of improvement in college students’ mental health, even as artificial intelligence takes on a growing role in young people’s personal and academic lives. Other findings highlight how economic concerns are shaping their political engagement and how early career exploration may help students build confidence in their futures.

Here are five findings from recent Inside Higher Ed Student Success coverage that shed light on how colleges and universities can better understand and support the current generation of students.

Student mental health is showing signs of improvement.

More than four in 10 American college students are flourishing—the highest share to report positive mental health in a decade, according to new survey data from the Healthy Minds Network. Meanwhile, rates of depression and anxiety have declined slightly as the stigma around discussing mental health wanes, though significant challenges remain.

The findings come from the 2025–26 Healthy Minds Study, led by researchers at Boston University; the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Michigan; and Wayne State University. The study includes responses from 67,477 students at 107 colleges and universities; 77 percent were between the ages of 18 and 25.

Among respondents, 43 percent were identified as flourishing, up from 38 percent the previous academic year. Meanwhile, 34 percent reported symptoms of depression, down from 37 percent, and 30 percent reported symptoms of anxiety, down from 32 percent. However, rates of suicidal ideation and self-harm remained largely unchanged, as did the share of those reporting symptoms of disordered eating (28 percent).

Still, the overall trend is encouraging, experts said.

“Just because someone is not reporting depressive symptoms does not necessarily mean that they are functioning at the highest level they can,” said Justin Heinze, a health and psychology professor at the University of Michigan and a co-author of the study. “So to have decreases in loneliness, increases in flourishing, to see decreases in perceived stigma—that’s all moving in a positive direction.”

Young people see AI as a safer source of emotional support.

Artificial intelligence has become increasingly intertwined with young people’s personal lives, including during their college years, when many are developing their identities and building meaningful relationships. But as AI becomes a source of emotional support and companionship, new research from The Rithm Project suggests that young people don’t necessarily have to trust the technology to turn to it for advice—they just need to perceive it as less risky than confiding in another person.

Earlier this year, the organization released research based on a survey of nearly 2,400 young people ages 13 to 24—including more than 500 young adults ages 18 to 24—examining how their AI use intersects with their social lives, emotional well-being and relationships.

In November, The Rithm Project released new research that builds on those findings through interviews with 29 young people from the original study—including 19 who are either currently enrolled in college or have completed a bachelor’s or associate degree. The interviews focused on two groups identified in the initial survey: those who turn to AI for personal and emotional support and those who interact with AI characters and personas.

Alison Lee, head of research and development at The Rithm Project, said one of the most notable findings was how young people weighed the perceived risks of confiding in AI against those of opening up to another person.

“What they were saying was ‘When I turn to AI, I know it’s hallucinating, I know that it’s glazing me, I know that it’s engaging in all these problematic behaviors,’” Lee said. “‘But those feel way more manageable as a risk than when I turn to a human.’

“Turning to a human is scary, it’s vulnerable, and you’re afraid of their judgment and emotional reactivity,” she added. “But big emotional events are a hallmark of the human experience … so it makes a lot of sense for young people to search for a place where those big emotions have a safe place to land and where they can make meaning of it.”

AI is changing college, but long-standing challenges remain.

The college experience is evolving as new technologies reshape how students learn, complete coursework and seek academic support. While AI helps some students navigate their education more efficiently, it has also introduced new concerns about academic integrity and the quality of learning.

According to Inside Higher Ed’s 2026–27 Student Voice survey of 5,034 undergraduates from 310 mostly public two- and four-year institutions, 34 percent of students say generative or agentic AI helps them complete coursework and study more efficiently, while 33 percent say it helps them feel more confident understanding and tackling difficult concepts. However, 25 percent say they have changed how they write to avoid being falsely flagged by AI detectors.

Despite these technological shifts, long-standing challenges continue to affect students’ academic success and persistence. Mental health is the most commonly cited barrier, reported by 41 percent of students, followed by financial pressure at 37 percent. More than six in 10 students have also gone without at least one essential—such as food, housing or transportation—in the past year for financial reasons.

Looking ahead, 54 percent of students want their institutions to prioritize job pipelines and internships to better prepare them for the labor market. At the same time, 80 percent somewhat or strongly agree that their college is preparing them to succeed in today’s job market, even as many report stress about life after graduation.

Economic concerns are shaping young voters’ priorities.

A variety of issues motivated young voters to head to the polls in the 2026 midterm elections, ranging from the economy and jobs to health care and the war in Iran. Their participation helped fuel historic levels of support for Democratic candidates, contributing to the party’s victories that shifted control of the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives.

New data from the Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE) at Tufts University found that the economy was the top issue for young voters in the 2026 midterm elections. Some 52 percent selected the economy and jobs as one of the three most important issues facing the country. Health care, another issue with significant economic implications, ranked second at 42 percent, followed by the war in Iran (27 percent), immigration (26 percent), education (21 percent) and climate change (20 percent).

Nationally, 66 percent of young voters ages 18 to 29 supported Democratic candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives, compared to 31 percent who supported Republicans. In several key states, the researchers found, young voters played a significant role in Democratic victories.

Leela Strong, the Newhouse executive director at CIRCLE, said during a postelection briefing that young men, rural youth and young people without a college degree—groups that helped President Trump win in 2024—were among those who shifted their support toward Democrats this year. She argued that the swing demonstrates that young voters, particularly Gen Z, are not necessarily driven by party loyalty or a single issue, but rather by a range of concerns.

“Young people, we know from all of our research, are not transactional voters,” Strong said. “They are acting on concerns about the economy and a democracy that isn’t working for their generation, and rewarding candidates who hear and see them.”

Early career exploration can build student confidence.

Introducing career exploration earlier in students’ academic journeys may help them develop a clearer sense of their professional interests and strengthen their motivation to stay enrolled and complete their degrees. That’s the idea behind Career Discovery, a for-credit course developed by Podium Education that gives first-year students opportunities to explore different industries and potential career paths through hands-on projects with employers.

The course, which eight universities piloted in the spring, connects students with real-world professional experiences, ranging from interviewing students about their consumer preferences for L’Oréal to completing marketing-related projects for other companies. In October, the educational technology company announced that the program had expanded to two additional institutions, bringing the total number of participating universities to 10.

Early findings from end-of-course student surveys suggest promising results. Students’ self-reported clarity about their strengths and interests more than doubled, while 80 percent reported greater career confidence. The share of students who said they intended to persist in college also increased by 15 percentage points.

Chris Parrish, co-founder and president of Podium Education, said the program was developed in response to growing concerns about the return on investment of a college degree and the need to make career exploration a priority earlier on for students.

“Many of the students we serve happen to be Pell [Grant recipients], happen to be first gen, but most freshmen haven’t been part of a boardroom before at a place like L’Oréal,” Parrish said. “Bringing the world of work and what it feels and looks like to them is a really important part of context setting, and that allows students to just have a seat at the table and to feel out what they like.”

title: Federal student lending caps are ‘blunt instrument’ to prevent defaults, researchers say
summary: Criteria such as program earnings and credit profiles would better address that risk, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia.
full_text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

Past graduate student loan recipients defaulted roughly twice as often when borrowing above levels recently capped by federal law compared to those borrowing below the limits, according to new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia’s Consumer Finance Institute.

Researchers also found that student borrowers’ credit risk scores strongly predicted their default rates. However, defaults were lower when the earnings potential of students’ programs were higher.

The researchers described the new borrowing caps as “a blunt instrument for screening out low-performing borrowers” and suggested a “richer set of criteria” including program earnings and credit profiles that would better address default risks than loan amounts.

Dive Insight:

The Republican spending bill enacted in 2025 ended the Grad PLUS lending program and set hard lifetime caps on federal student lending at $100,000 for graduate students and $200,000 for professional students — a classification being disputed in court.

Republicans aimed to reduce student debt loads through the law. When it passed, Rep. Tim Walberg, the Republican chair of the House Education and Workforce Committee, said the loan overhaul would help ensure “students don’t borrow excessive debt they can never repay.”

To examine the potential impact of the caps, the Philadelphia Fed research looked at three-year default rates among borrowers who took out federal graduate student loans and entered repayment between 2011 and 2016.

The overall default rate for those borrowing over the new limits — in inflation-adjusted dollars pegged to 2025 — of 6.5% for graduate students compares to a 3.3% rate for those borrowing below the limits. Master’s students drove up that rate, as they defaulted 7.2% of the time when borrowing above loan cap levels.

But the size of students’ federal loans wasn’t the only factor that predicted defaults.

Another was borrowers’ credit risk profiles. Three-year default rates for all graduate borrowers declined as their credit scores improved, the Philadelphia Fed found.

Borrowers with credit scores between 300 and 579 — deemed “deep subprime” — defaulted at a 12.4% rate. That rate declined until it reached just half a percent for those with scores between 770 to 850, the highest credit scores.

In every credit score bracket, students who borrowed above the new limits defaulted more often than those who borrowed less than the capped levels.

But those credit profiles don’t tell the full story, the researchers noted. The earnings potential of students’ fields of study also played a major role in defaults. Sub-prime and near-prime borrowers who studied in the highest-earning programs defaulted less frequently than less-risky prime borrowers in lower-earning programs.

“Loan limits are a far coarser signal of loan performance than either creditworthiness or program characteristics,” the researchers wrote.

But under the new caps, riskier student borrowers could be locked out of higher-earning programs by a private lending market that is expected to take over a larger share of student lending.

Following the Democratic sweep of the midterm elections, the federal loan caps could come under political pressure. Rep. Bobby Scott, the ranking Democratic member of the House education committee, has blasted the federal loan caps.

In March, for example, he and other Democrats on the committee said that the lending structure will “further restrict higher education access, particularly for low- and middle-income borrowers” and “destabilizes our higher education system and harms students.”

title: Universities urged to rethink expansion at Going Global 2026
summary:
University leaders at Going Global 2026 called for institutions to rethink and innovate their models, warning that increased growth alone doesn’t automatically improve education quality.

The post Universities urged to rethink expansion at Going Global 2026 appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Higher education has seen rapid growth over the past two decades worldwide, with the number of students enrolled in higher education worldwide increasing from about 100 million in 2000 to 269 million in 2024, according to data from UNESCO earlier this year.

But sector leaders in Istanbul last week warned that institutions need to look beyond growth figures and ask if this growth has actually had a positive impact on teaching.

Komiljon Karimov, rector of the Westminster International University in Tashkent, said that expanding higher education was an “economic necessity, social priority, and fundamentally a matter of opportunity,” in particular for many first-generation students.

But he added that “creating more university places does not automatically mean creating better educational experiences… Expansion changes the size of a system, but transformation changes what that system is capable of achieving.”

A recurring theme throughout the conference was that numbers are often perceived as the main indicator of success.

Mehmet Naci İnci, rector at Boğaziçi University, said the higher education sector is “addicted to counting” whether it’s “the number of students, the number of cases or the number of agreements… We are not yet ready to change that habit, unfortunately.”

He said that institutions must look beyond the numbers and ask themselves if growth has actually made their teaching better or science stronger.

Naci İnci argued that, as higher education expands internationally, institutions need to focus on building stronger partnerships rather than simply increasing the number of agreements they sign.

“Our strongest partnerships did not start with big publicity ceremonies. They were the ones that lasted for years. Two scientists working on the same problem, supervising PhD students together, building trust step by step… those partnerships worked because they left behind real results, better courses, stronger labs, and young researchers leading their own teams”, he added.

The greatest risk is “not that higher education systems will stop growing, but they will continue growing without changing sufficiently.”

Komiljon Karimov, rector of the Westminster International University

Panellists agreed that now, more than ever, with technological advancement and artificial intelligence transforming how knowledge is produced, how professionals work and what employers expect, higher education systems need to adapt.

Lisa Roberts, vice-chancellor of the University of Exeter, argued that as higher education expands, universities must ensure their education remains relevant to a changing labour market. With AI reshaping the world of work, she said institutions need to “think differently and transform” quickly to prepare students for the future.

She described this as a “challenging” task for institutions.

Karimov similarly questioned whether universities are “preparing students for the jobs of tomorrow or for the jobs we understood yesterday,” as many university programs still follow “relatively fixed” curricula, disciplinary boundaries, and assessment models.

Graduates need to be able to “interpret unfamiliar problems, exercise judgment and work with technology,” he said.

Karimov also highlighted the pressure on institutions to “educate more students, maintain academic standards, adopt technological change, and contribute more directly to economic development” all at the same time.

He questioned whether sufficient investment had been made in academic staff, institutional leadership and governance to help universities manage these demands and build their capacity for change.

The greatest risk is “not that higher education systems will stop growing, but they will continue growing without changing sufficiently”, he said.

title: Teaching empathy through soft systems thinking
summary: by Amrik Singh and Joy Garfield Empathy is often described as a personal quality, but in higher education it should be understood as a teachable educational practice. In a world shaped by complexity and competing stakeholder interests, students need more … Continue reading →
full_text:
by Amrik Singh and Joy Garfield

Empathy is often described as a personal quality, but in higher education it should be understood as a teachable educational practice. In a world shaped by complexity and competing stakeholder interests, students need more than technical knowledge. They need to understand how people experience problems, why people interpret the same situation differently, and how decisions affect voices that may be overlooked. They need to understand stakeholder worldviews. Students need to understand the importance of being able to relate to people rather than just relying on GenAI.

At Aston Business School, Soft Systems Methodology (SSM) makes empathy practical. Rather than treating empathy as a vague aspiration, SSM gives students a structured method for exploring human-centred problems through stakeholder perspectives, worldviews and tensions. It helps them move from asking “what is the solution?” to asking “who is affected, what matters to them, and how do they understand the situation?”

Why empathy matters in student learning

Empathy enables students to see beyond their own assumptions. Every organisational or social problem is experienced differently depending on role, values, responsibilities and pressures. A manager may view change as necessary for efficiency, while employees may experience it as threatening or poorly communicated. Empathy helps students notice these differences before they rush to judgement.

Students often approach learning tasks as if there is one correct answer. In case studies, group projects and consultancy simulations, they may search quickly for a recommendation or framework. Yet real-world problems are messy because people interpret them through different worldviews. They are complex and ambiguous. Empathy gives students permission to slow down, listen, question and understand before proposing solutions. SSM allows students to do this.

Empathy is more than being kind

One challenge in teaching empathy is that it can be misunderstood as simply being nice, agreeable or sympathetic. In professional education, empathy must be more disciplined. It involves attention to meaning, emotion, context and consequence, reflecting empathy as a multidimensional system rather than a single trait (Guthridge and Giummarra, 2021). It requires students to ask what people need, what they value and what they may not feel able to say openly.

How Soft Systems Methodology Makes Empathy Actionable

Soft Systems Methodology is useful because it was designed for complex human situations with multiple perspectives and no single agreed definition of the problem. In teaching, this makes it a powerful vehicle for empathy. Students explore stakeholders, relationships, worldviews and possible accommodations before reaching conclusions (Checkland and Poulter, 2006). Through SSM, students ask: Who is affected? What are their worldviews? What tensions exist between stakeholder groups? What does improvement mean from each perspective? What assumptions are shaping the issue? These questions move empathy from good intention to structured inquiry.

In a consultancy classroom, students may analyse a complex organisational or social challenge. A traditional approach might focus quickly on performance data or strategic recommendations. An empathetic SSM approach begins by considering how the situation is experienced by different stakeholders. Students learn that each group or individual may hold differing world views. They learn this through role plays and simulation of interviews between stakeholders and consultants. This allows them to dig deeper into the issues, concerns, feelings and worldviews of the stakeholders.

Rich pictures and the practice of seeing through others’ eyes

One effective SSM tool for developing empathy is the rich picture. Rich pictures ask students to represent a situation visually, including people, processes, relationships, conflicts and issues/concerns. The value is not artistic quality; it is the thinking and dialogue behind the image (Checkland and Poulter, 2006).

When students construct a rich picture, they decide what to include and why. They consider who has power, who feels pressure, where communication breaks down and where different interpretations emerge. This encourages them to see the problem as a living system of people, interests and meanings.

Rich pictures also support group dialogue. Students challenge one another’s assumptions: Are we missing someone? Have we shown conflict fairly? Have we assumed what people think without listening properly? These conversations help empathy develop in the classroom.

Embedding empathy through learning design

To teach empathy effectively, it must be designed into learning activities such as stakeholder role plays, questioning, interviews, reflective dialogue, and structured group work. Students can adopt stakeholder positions, interview each other, reflect on misunderstandings and revisit their analysis after hearing alternative perspectives. Such activities work best when scaffolded with prompts, templates and examples. Over time, support can be reduced as students gain confidence. Empathy is not developed through a single activity; it grows through repeated practice, reflection and feedback.

Assessment can reinforce empathetic learning. Rather than rewarding only the final recommendation, educators can assess how well students understand stakeholder perspectives, justify assumptions, acknowledge tensions and reflect on their own learning.

Preparing students for human-centred futures

As artificial intelligence and digital technologies reshape work, empathy becomes even more important. Employers need graduates who combine analytical capability with human judgement. Technology may process information, but students still need to interpret context, build trust and make responsible decisions where people disagree. Ultimately, empathy is not separate from academic rigour. It deepens rigour by asking students to consider evidence, meaning, context and consequence together. When students learn empathy through Soft Systems Methodology, they become better equipped to understand complex situations and develop solutions that are technically sound, socially aware and ethically responsible.

Dr Amrik Singh is a Senior Teaching Fellow at Aston University, UK. He has 20 years of academic experience in Higher Education. He is also a Senior Fellow of the Advance HE, SFHEA. His teaching areas includes operations management, and effective management consultancy. Research interests include supply chain risk management, and information flows in the supply chain. He has a pedagogical interest in the applications of Soft Systems Methodology (SSM) in teaching and learning. This includes applying systems thinking and SSM to various operations, business and management consultancy contexts.

Dr Joy Garfield is Associate Dean for Education and Student Experience (MBA and Executive Education) at Aston Business School, Aston University, UK. Her subject discipline area is information systems, particularly systems modelling and complex problem solving. With 25 years of experience in academia, she has worked at a number of UK universities. Joy is a Senior Fellow of Advance HE and is currently an external examiner at Westminster International University, Uzbekistan.

title: Participarea ministrului Educației și Cercetării, Valentin-Sorin Costreie, la reuniunea Consiliului Educație, Tineret, Cultură și Sport - secțiunea Educație (19 noiembrie 2026)
summary:
Participarea ministrului Educației și Cercetării, Valentin-Sorin Costreie, la reuniunea Consiliului Educație, Tineret, Cultură și Sport - secțiunea Educație (19 noiembrie 2026)
Mon, 23 Nov 2026 - 12:00
daniel.tomoni Mon, 23 Nov 2026 - 16:03
Etichete
comunicate de presă
Categorie
Comunicate de presă
full_text:
O delegație a Ministerului Educației și Cercetării, condusă de ministrul Educației și Cercetării, Valentin-Sorin Costreie, a participat, în data de 19 noiembrie 2026, la reuniunea Consiliului Educație, Tineret, Cultură și Sport (EYCS) - secțiunea Educație, prezidată de Irlanda, deținătoarea președinției rotative la Consiliul Uniunii Europene.

În cadrul sesiunii publice, miniștrii Educației din statele membre au adoptat două documente non-legislative, negociate și finalizate în cadrul Președinției irlandeze a Consiliului:

Propunere de Concluzii ale Consiliului privind educația și formarea în domeniul STEM (Știință, Tehnologie, Inginerie și Matematică), disponibil aici.

Concluziile adoptate evidențiază o serie de provocări comune la nivel european, precum deficitul de cadre didactice calificate în domeniile STEM, necesitatea îmbunătățirii rezultatelor învățării, participarea redusă a fetelor și a femeilor, precum și barierele întâmpinate de persoanele provenite din medii socioeconomice dezavantajate sau de cursanții cu nevoi diverse. În acest context, statele membre sunt invitate să promoveze participarea la educația STEM, să dezvolte strategii naționale sau regionale în domeniu, să consolideze orientarea școlară și profesională, să sprijine formarea inițială și continuă a profesorilor, a formatorilor și a liderilor educaționali și să încurajeze cooperarea între furnizorii de educație și formare, mediul economic, cercetare și industrie.

Propunere de Concluzii ale Consiliului privind competențele și abilitățile necesare pentru a interacționa cu inteligența artificială (IA) - disponibil aici.

Documentul adoptat recunoaște atât potențialul IA de a sprijini accesul la cunoaștere, inovarea și îmbunătățirea proceselor de predare și învățare, cât și provocările asociate utilizării IA, precum: protecția datelor, integritatea academică, dezinformarea, prejudecățile algoritmice, dependența excesivă, efectele negative asupra abilităților cognitive și menționează faptul că predarea-învățarea trebuie să rămână centrate pe factorul uman. În acest context, statele membre sunt invitate să adopte o abordare coerentă, incluzivă și fundamentată pe dovezi pentru a sprijini formarea competențelor necesare utilizării IA, prin reflecție continuă, cooperare, colaborare și dialog între factorii de decizie și toate părțile interesate relevante.

Un element central al reuniunii Consiliului EYCS l-a constituit schimbul de opinii dedicat temei Gândire critică, decizia umană și educația și formarea profesională într-un mediu digital în schimbare. În intervenția sa, ministrul român al educației a reflectat asupra riscului reducerii capacităților cognitive umane în contextul expansiunii rapide a inteligenței artificiale, subliniind importanța educației reflexive și a regândirii modului de predare pentru formarea gândirii critice.

Un punct de interes l-a constituit punctul de informare propus de România și susținut de șapte state membre, dedicat educației și competențelor pentru reziliență democratică. Ministrul educației și cercetării a subliniat rolul central al educației pentru a le oferi elevilor cunoștințe, abilități, atitudini și valori care îi ancorează într-un context istoric și într-o societate democratică bazată pe valori, ceea ce conferă o protecție solidă împotriva manipulării online, a dezinformării și a informațiilor eronate. Abordarea propusă este una comprehensivă, incluzând competențe de bază solide pentru toți, consolidarea educației pentru cetățenie democratică, alfabetizarea media și digitală, gândirea critică, formarea cadrelor didactice, competențe socioemoționale și un mediu de învățare sigur, incluziv, favorabil și pozitiv, care încurajează participarea activă a elevilor și sentimentul de apartenență.

În cadrul aceleiași sesiuni, România a sprijinit punctul de informare privind siguranța online a copiilor împotriva radicalizării, ca parte a eforturilor la nivel european de introducere a unui prag minim de vârstă pentru accesarea platformelor sociale prin intermediul propunerii de regulament privind protecția copiilor în mediul online (EU KIDS Act), și a extins miniștrilor educației din statele membre invitația de a participa la Conferința ministerială a Spațiului European pentru Învățământ Superior organizată la Iași și Chișinău în perioada 26 - 27 mai 2027.

Programul de lucru al delegației Ministerului Educației și Cercetării a inclus și întâlniri cu domnul Siegfried Mureșan, co-raportor al Parlamentului European pentru cadrul financiar 2028 - 2034, domnul Nicolae Ștefănuță, membru al Comisiei PE pentru industrie, transporturi și cercetare, precum și o întâlnire la nivel de expert cu delegația Ungariei pe tema educației prin artă. Temele abordate au inclus utilizarea actualului cadru financiar european pentru a răspunde nevoilor sistemului românesc de educație, nevoia de investiții în infrastructura socială universitară (cămine și cantine), precum și viitorul programului Erasmus+.

Participarea delegației Ministerului Educației și Cercetării la Summitul european privind educația și competențele: Școli pentru viitor: școli pregătite pentru era Inteligenței Artificiale, 20 noiembrie 2026

În a doua zi a vizitei delegației Ministerului Educației și Cercetării la Bruxelles, ministrul Valentin-Sorin Costreie a participat ca speaker în cadrul celei de-a treia sesiuni plenare organizate în cadrul Summitului european dedicat educației și competențelor.

Sesiunea a avut în centru investițiile de calitate pentru asigurarea rezervei de talente a Europei în sprijinul competitivității și al rezilienței.

Summitul european este evenimentul anual emblematic al Spațiului European al Educației în contextul Uniunii Competențelor, organizat de Comisia Europeană, și oferă o platformă la nivel înalt pentru un dialog deschis care modelează educația în Europa și nu numai. Ediția din acest an a fost dedicată pregătirii școlilor pentru viitor pregătite în era inteligenței artificiale și a avut loc în contextul adoptării pachetului pentru educație al Comisiei Europene.

De asemenea, în marja Summitului, ministrul Sorin Costreie a avut întâlniri de lucru cu secretarul de stat responsabil pentru educație, doamna Judith Tielen, pentru o discuție introductivă privind prioritățile și aranjamentele de guvernanță ale noului consorțiu EDIC EDU, în vederea începerii discuțiilor pentru participarea României, cu domnul Joao Costa, directorul Agenției europene pentru educație incluzivă și pentru nevoi speciale (EASNIE), căreia România i se va alătura ca membru de la 1 ianuarie 2027, precum și cu domnul Daniel Wisnievski, secretar general al Federației europene a angajatorilor din educație (EFEE).

Din delegația MEC a făcut parte și Camelia Mircea-Sturza, consilier pentru afaceri europene.
